lesson.title: Labor, Tribute, and the Machinery of Conquest
lesson.summary: The encomienda system let Spanish colonists extract forced labor and tribute from indigenous communities in the name of protection and conversion, becoming one of the most consequential and abusive institutions of early Spanish colonization.
lesson.body:
Once Spanish conquistadors had subdued a region, whether Hernan Cortes's conquest of the Aztec empire in 1519 to 1521 or Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca empire beginning in 1532, the crown faced a practical question: how would a small number of Spanish colonists control and profit from a vastly larger indigenous population spread across enormous territory. The encomienda system, first formalized in instructions issued for Hispaniola around 1503, offered an answer that predated and then expanded alongside these later conquests.

Under the system, the Spanish crown granted a colonist, called an encomendero, the right to demand labor and tribute from the indigenous people of a specified area. In exchange, the encomendero was supposed to provide protection and instruction in the Catholic faith. In theory this was a reciprocal arrangement rooted in medieval Iberian traditions of lordship. In practice, encomenderos frequently treated the grant as a license for forced labor with almost no oversight, working indigenous people in mines, fields, and households under conditions that differed from outright slavery mainly in name.

The human cost was severe and compounded a catastrophe that was already unfolding for another reason entirely. Indigenous populations across the Caribbean and Mesoamerica were dying in staggering numbers from diseases like smallpox and measles, illnesses to which they had no prior immunity because these pathogens had crossed the Atlantic with the Spanish rather than having circulated in the Americas before. The encomienda system layered brutal forced labor on top of this demographic collapse, pushing already devastated communities toward further decline as sick and starving people were still compelled to work.

Opposition emerged from within the Spanish colonial and religious establishment itself. Bartolome de las Casas, a Dominican friar who had once held an encomienda himself before renouncing it, became the system's most persistent critic, documenting abuses in detailed accounts sent back to Spain and arguing that indigenous people were rational beings entitled to just treatment under natural law. His advocacy contributed to the New Laws issued by Charles V in 1542, which attempted to phase out the encomienda system and prohibit new grants.

The New Laws provoked fierce resistance from colonists whose fortunes depended on forced labor, and enforcement in distant colonies proved weak; the encomienda persisted in modified forms in some regions for generations. But the system's basic economic logic, the need for a large, controllable labor force to work mines and plantations as indigenous populations continued to fall, pushed Spanish and Portuguese colonizers toward an alternative source of forced labor that would prove even more destructive: the trans-Atlantic trade in enslaved Africans.
